questions.q: What is the first step when you encounter something you do not understand in science?
questions.a: The first step is to observe the situation carefully. A wrong answer, such as "guessing the answer immediately," shows the student lacks patience for observation, which is the foundation of scientific inquiry.

questions.q: Why do we call the process of testing an idea an "experiment"?
questions.a: An experiment is a test designed to see if our guess about how the world works is correct or wrong. A wrong answer like "it is just following a rule" shows the student thinks science is about memorizing steps rather than discovering truths through evidence.

questions.q: If your torch stops glowing, how would you use the scientific method to fix it?
questions.a: First, observe the torch; then, guess it might be the battery; next, test it by replacing the battery; finally, see if it glows. If the student jumps to "buy a new one," they have missed the testing/inquiry phase of the scientific method.

questions.q: Compare the roles of curiosity and evidence in scientific temper.
questions.a: Curiosity is the spark that makes us ask the question, while evidence is the proof that confirms our answer. If a student says "they are the same," they fail to distinguish between the desire to know and the scientific requirement of proof.

questions.q: Is a person who cooks food following the scientific method if they change the amount of salt to improve taste?
questions.a: Yes, because they are observing the result of their previous attempt, forming a new hypothesis (less/more salt), and testing it in the next batch. A "no" answer reveals a misunderstanding that science only happens in labs.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment to find out if ice melts faster in sunlight or in the shade.
questions.a: The answer must include: taking two identical ice cubes, placing one in sun and one in shade, and recording the time taken for each to melt. A poor answer fails to keep the ice cubes identical, showing a lack of understanding of "fair testing."

questions.q: Fill in the blank: ______ temper is a way of thinking that involves being curious, observing the world carefully, and using evidence to test our ideas instead of relying on guesses.
Fill in the blank: Have you ever wondered why your plant in the corner is ______ while the one on the balcony is growing tall?
What is Scientific temper? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Scientific temper is a way of thinking that involves being curious, observing the world carefully, and using evidence to test our ideas instead of relying on guesses.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Scientific temper?
questions.a: Students often believe science is only for experts in white coats in laboratories.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to identify a problem, propose a testable hypothesis, and describe an experiment to verify that hypothesis in a daily-life situation.
